mainTopic: Which opinion the oath משנה follows, and whether רבי עקיבא holds that eating any amount brings liability everywhere or only with oaths
overview: The גמרא first looks at the words "זו היא" ("this is") at the end of the משנה about שבועת שוא and asks what they come to exclude. After going back and forth, it concludes that the whole משנה follows רבי עקיבא, because a line about future oaths should exclude a future case. Next it turns to רבי עקיבא's ruling that someone who swore not to eat is liable for eating any amount. It asks whether רבי עקיבא holds like רבי שמעון, that a tiny amount brings liability everywhere, or only rules this way for oaths. One proof from the משנה is pushed off, but proofs from a נזיר who soaked bread in wine and from ריש לקיש's explanation of an oath on forbidden foods show that, in general, רבי עקיבא holds like the רבנן. Finally the גמרא tests the רבנן's question "where do we find liability for any amount?" with an ant, הקדש, and a clearly stated oath, and answers each one. The case of dirt cannot be answered that way, so the גמרא begins to reword the רבנן's question, and this continues on the next amud.

steps.title: What does "this is" exclude in the line about vain oaths?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the end of the משנה about שבועת שוא and asks what the words "זו היא" come to exclude. It suggests they exclude an oath about the past ("I ate" or "I did not eat") from getting מלקות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Look at the end of the משנה: "This is a vain oath: you get lashes if you swore it on purpose, and you are exempt if you swore it by mistake." What does "this is" come to leave out? Isn't it leaving out someone who swore "I ate" or "I did not eat", teaching that he does not get lashes?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a line from the end of the משנה and tries to read something out of the words "זו היא". It suggests those words teach that a false oath about the past does not get מלקות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Words like "זו היא" ("this is") sound like they limit the rule to this case only. The גמרא suggests the case being left out is an oath about the past ("I ate" / "I did not eat"). If that is right, such an oath would carry no מלקות.

keyTerms.meaning: Look at the end of the משנה
A vain oath, such as swearing that something everyone knows is true is false
Doing it on purpose / doing it by mistake
What does it come to leave out?
He gets lashes (מלקות)

phrases.english: Say the end of the משנה:
This is a vain oath,
for which one is liable to lashes if done on purpose,
and if done by mistake, he is exempt.
"This is" comes to exclude what?
Isn't it to exclude
"I ate" and "I did not eat"
that he does not get lashes?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier discussion of whether a false oath about the past gets מלקות, now using the end of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that a false oath about the past ("I ate" / "I did not eat") gets מלקות
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: "זו היא" seems to exclude something. The most natural thing to exclude is an oath about the past, which would mean it gets no מלקות.

steps.title: No — "this is" excludes a vain oath from a קרבן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the reading. "זו היא" teaches that a vain oath sworn by mistake brings no קרבן. But a mistaken oath of "I ate" or "I did not eat" does bring a קרבן, following רבי עקיבא, who treats oaths about the past like oaths about the future.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. "This is" means that only this oath, when sworn by mistake, is exempt from a קרבן. But "I ate" or "I did not eat" sworn by mistake does require a קרבן. This follows רבי עקיבא, who makes a person liable for oaths about the past just like oaths about the future.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back and says the words "זו היא" are about the קרבן, not about מלקות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exclusion now points the other way. The vain oath is the case that has no קרבן when sworn by mistake, while past-tense oaths like "I ate" do bring one. That only works according to רבי עקיבא, who brings a קרבן even for oaths about the past.

keyTerms.meaning: The offering brought for a mistaken false oath
About the past
About the future

steps.confusionAlert: Watch the switch. Step 1 read the exclusion as being about מלקות. Here it is about the קרבן. The very same words are given a completely different job.

phrases.english: No; "this is" means
that for doing it by mistake, he is exempt from an offering,
but "I ate" and "I did not eat"
when sworn by mistake, he is liable to an offering;
and this is רבי עקיבא,
who makes one liable for the past like for the future.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא; זוֹ הִיא דְּעַל שִׁגְגָתָהּ פָּטוּר מִקׇּרְבָּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects step 1's reading of "זו היא" and offers a different one.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that "זו היא" excludes past-tense oaths from מלקות
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The words can just as well be read as excluding the vain oath from a קרבן, so the משנה does not show that past-tense oaths get no מלקות.

steps.title: A split משנה? First half רבי ישמעאל, second half רבי עקיבא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects. Earlier we said the first part of the משנה follows רבי ישמעאל. Can the first part be רבי ישמעאל and the end be רבי עקיבא?
steps.simpleTranslation: But you said the first part is רבי ישמעאל! Is the first part רבי ישמעאל and the end רבי עקיבא?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the answer in step 2 clashes with what was said earlier about the first part of the same משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the first part ("זו היא שבועת ביטוי") was explained as following רבי ישמעאל, who brings no קרבן for oaths about the past. Step 2 now says the end follows רבי עקיבא, who disagrees. It is very hard to say one משנה switches between two opposing opinions.

keyTerms.meaning: But you said!
The first part of the משנה

phrases.aramaic: הָא אָמְרַתְּ רֵישָׁא רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל הִיא!
phrases.english: But you said the first part is רבי ישמעאל!
phrases.notes: The first part is the matching line about שבועת ביטוי, which the גמרא earlier explained following רבי ישמעאל.

phrases.aramaic: רֵישָׁא רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל וְסֵיפָא רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא?!
phrases.english: The first part רבי ישמעאל and the end רבי עקיבא?!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא אָמְרַתְּ רֵישָׁא רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 2 because it makes the משנה inconsistent.
steps.kashyaTarget: Step 2's claim that the end of the משנה follows רבי עקיבא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It is unlikely that one משנה follows רבי ישמעאל in its first part and רבי עקיבא, who disagrees with him, in its end.

steps.title: The whole משנה is רבי עקיבא; the first part excludes "I will eat" from מלקות
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the whole משנה follows רבי עקיבא. In the first part, "זו היא" does not exclude "I ate" from a קרבן. It excludes someone who swore "I will eat" and then did not eat from getting מלקות. He still brings a קרבן.
steps.simpleTranslation: The whole משנה is רבי עקיבא. The first part does not come to exclude "I ate" and "I did not eat" from a קרבן. It comes to exclude "I will eat" (when he then did not eat) from lashes. But he is still liable to a קרבן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא solves the clash by re-reading the first part of the משנה so that it also follows רבי עקיבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exclusion in the first part is now about מלקות, not the קרבן. The case being excluded is a future oath that was broken by not doing anything ("I will eat" and he did not eat). That case gets no מלקות but still brings a קרבן, so the whole משנה fits רבי עקיבא.

keyTerms.meaning: All of it, the whole משנה
"I will eat", and then he did not eat
Lashes
He is liable

steps.whatToRemember: In the end the whole משנה follows רבי עקיבא. The first "זו היא" excludes "I will eat" (and he did not eat) from מלקות. The second "זו היא" excludes the vain oath from a קרבן.

phrases.english: All of it is רבי עקיבא,
and the first part is not to exclude
"I ate" and "I did not eat" from an offering,
but to exclude "I will eat" and he did not eat from lashes,
but he is liable to an offering.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of step 3 by re-reading the first part of the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the source so one opinion fits the whole משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The first part follows רבי ישמעאל and excludes past-tense oaths from a קרבן.
steps.terutzMaskana: The first part follows רבי עקיבא and excludes "I will eat" (not done) from מלקות only.

steps.title: Why is this reading better?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what makes the new reading of the first part better than the old one.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is the difference?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why we should prefer the new reading. It is setting up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both readings could explain the words "זו היא". The גמרא wants a reason, other than avoiding a split משנה, that shows the new reading fits the text better.

keyTerms.meaning: And what is the difference? Why prefer this?

phrases.english: And what is different?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the answer given in step 4.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the new reading of the first part is to be preferred

steps.title: A line about the future should exclude a future case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that it makes sense this way. When the משנה is talking about future oaths, its exclusion should also be a future oath. It would be odd for it to be talking about the future and exclude a case about the past.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense: when it is dealing with the future, it excludes a future case. Would it deal with the future and exclude a past case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a common-sense reason why the new reading is better. It concludes the discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first part of the משנה is talking about oaths about the future. So the exclusion in it is most naturally another future case, "I will eat". The old reading had it excluding a past case ("I ate"), which does not match what the line is talking about.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense
It is standing in, dealing with
Excludes, leaves out

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common way the גמרא reads extra words like "זו היא": an exclusion should usually come from the same kind of case the line is talking about.

phrases.english: It makes sense: dealing with the future, it excludes the future;
dealing with the future, would it exclude the past?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A line about future oaths should exclude a future case ("I will eat"), not a past case ("I ate"). So the reading in which the whole משנה is רבי עקיבא is better.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The whole משנה follows רבי עקיבא. In the first part, "זו היא" excludes "I will eat" (and he did not eat) from מלקות.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: an oath not to eat, and he ate a tiny amount
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the line of the משנה where someone swore not to eat and then ate any amount, and is liable according to רבי עקיבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'An oath that I will not eat,' and he ate any amount, he is liable, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by quoting a line from the משנה. It is setting up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the opinion of רבי עקיבא: even less than a כזית counts as breaking an oath of 'I will not eat.' The רבנן in the משנה disagree and require a כזית. The גמרא now wants to know why רבי עקיבא says this.

keyTerms.meaning: An oath
Any amount at all, even a tiny bit
Liable (gets a punishment or must bring a קרבן)

phrases.english: "An oath that I will not eat," and he ate any amount,
he is liable, etc.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁלֹּא אוֹכַל וְאָכַל כׇּל שֶׁהוּא, חַיָּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic in the משנה after the discussion about past and future oaths.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי עקיבא, one who swore not to eat and then ate any amount is liable.

steps.title: Does רבי עקיבא hold like רבי שמעון everywhere?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether רבי עקיבא holds, for the whole תורה, that eating any amount brings liability, like רבי שמעון in a ברייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: Does רבי עקיבא hold like רבי שמעון in the whole תורה, that a person is liable for eating even a tiny amount? As a ברייתא teaches: רבי שמעון says any amount is enough for מלקות, and a כזית was only said for a קרבן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises an open question (איבעיא) about the reason behind רבי עקיבא's opinion. This is the first side of the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Maybe רבי עקיבא's ruling has nothing special to do with oaths. Maybe he simply agrees with רבי שמעון that in every eating prohibition, any amount brings מלקות. A כזית would then only matter for a קרבן.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked among the scholars (an open question)
A tiny bit, any amount
Lashes (מלקות)
The size of an olive, the usual minimum amount for eating
An offering brought to the בית המקדש

phrases.english: A question was asked of them:
Rabbi Akiva, in the entire Torah,
phrases.notes: He means in every eating prohibition, not only with oaths.

phrases.english: does he hold like Rabbi Shimon,
who makes a person liable for any tiny amount?
As it was taught: Rabbi Shimon says:
Any amount is enough for lashes,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא אָמְרוּ כְּזַיִת אֶלָּא לְעִנְיַן קׇרְבָּן.
phrases.english: and they only said an olive-size for the matter of an offering.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, בְּכׇל הַתּוֹרָה כּוּלָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the משנה's ruling just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is רבי עקיבא's ruling based on a general view, like רבי שמעון, that any amount brings liability everywhere?

steps.title: Why the argument appears here and not in general
steps.stepSummary: Still on the first side: if רבי עקיבא agrees with רבי שמעון everywhere, why does the משנה put the argument here? To show how far the רבנן go: even with oaths they exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really they should have argued about the general rule. The reason they argue here is to show the strength of the רבנן's view. Someone might say: since a person who clearly said 'even a tiny bit' is liable, a person who just said 'I will not eat' is also liable. The משנה teaches us that the רבנן still exempt him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers a question hiding inside the first side: if this is a general argument, why place it in the topic of oaths?
steps.deeperAnalysis: With oaths there is a special reason to be strict, because someone who clearly swore off 'even a tiny bit' is liable. Placing the argument here shows that the רבנן exempt even in this harder case. So the placement teaches something about the רבנן, not about רבי עקיבא.

keyTerms.meaning: In general, everywhere
The strength, how far the רבנן's view goes
One who states it clearly (swore off even a tiny amount)
Plainly, without stating details
It teaches us

steps.confusionAlert: Both the רבנן and רבי עקיבא agree that someone who clearly swore 'not even a tiny bit' is liable for a tiny bit. They only argue about a plain oath of 'I will not eat.'

phrases.english: And by right they should have argued in general,
and the reason they argue here
is to let you know the strength of the Rabbis,
that even though one could say:
since one who specifies is liable,
phrases.notes: That's someone who said clearly, 'I swear I won't eat even a tiny bit.'

phrases.english: one who swears plainly is also liable;
it teaches us that they exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends the first side of the question by explaining why the משנה places the argument with oaths.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the משנה's choice of case as showing the strength of the רבנן.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If רבי עקיבא holds like רבי שמעון everywhere, the משנה should have stated the argument in general terms.
steps.terutzMaskana: The argument is placed with oaths to show that the רבנן exempt even where there is a reason to be strict.

steps.title: The other side: maybe רבי עקיבא agrees with the רבנן in general
steps.stepSummary: Or perhaps רבי עקיבא requires a כזית in general, and here his reason is special to oaths: a plain oath is treated like a clearly stated one.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or perhaps, in general he holds like the רבנן. Here this is the reason: since one who clearly said 'even a tiny bit' is liable, one who swore plainly is also liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the second side of its question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On this side, רבי עקיבא's ruling is only about oaths. A plain 'I will not eat' is understood to include even a tiny bit, just like someone who said so clearly. In other eating prohibitions, he would need a כזית.

keyTerms.meaning: Or perhaps (introduces the second side of a question)
He holds, that is his view
This is the reason

phrases.english: Or perhaps, in general,
he holds like the Rabbis;
and here, this is the reason:
since one who specifies is liable,
one who swears plainly is also liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אוֹ דִלְמָא, בְּעָלְמָא – כְּרַבָּנַן סְבִירָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the second possibility of the question begun in step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Or is רבי עקיבא's ruling limited to oaths, because a plain oath counts like a clearly stated one?
steps.whyThisMatters: This decides whether רבי עקיבא's opinion is a rule about all eating prohibitions or only a rule about how we understand oaths.

steps.title: The proof: what the רבנן said to רבי עקיבא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings what the רבנן said to רבי עקיבא: where do we ever find that eating any amount makes one liable, that you say this one is liable?
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: the רבנן said to רבי עקיבא, 'Where do we find that someone who eats any amount is liable, that you say this person is liable?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source to help answer its question. Here it quotes the source; the next step explains how it proves something.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן argued that nowhere in the תורה is eating a tiny amount punished. This suggests that, in their discussion, eating any amount was not an accepted rule anywhere.

keyTerms.meaning: Where do we find?

phrases.english: Come and hear:
for they said to Rabbi Akiva:

phrases.aramaic: הֵיכָן מָצִינוּ בְּאוֹכֵל כָּל שֶׁהוּא חַיָּיב,
phrases.english: Where do we find that one who eats any amount is liable,
that this one should be liable?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּאָמְרוּ לוֹ לְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to decide between the two sides of the question.
steps.raayaObject: Which side of the question is correct about רבי עקיבא's general view.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The challenge of the רבנן to רבי עקיבא: 'Where do we find that one who eats any amount is liable?'

steps.title: Why רבי עקיבא's silence shows he does not hold like רבי שמעון
steps.stepSummary: If רבי עקיבא held like רבי שמעון everywhere, he should have answered: 'In the whole תורה I hold like רבי שמעון!' Since he did not, it seems he agrees with the רבנן in general.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it were so, let him say to them: 'I hold like רבי שמעון in the whole תורה!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how the quote proves its point: רבי עקיבא had an easy answer and did not give it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If רבי עקיבא believed any amount brings liability everywhere, the רבנן's question 'where do we find this?' would not bother him. He could just say he follows רבי שמעון. Since he did not, the proof points to the second side: his ruling is only about oaths.

keyTerms.meaning: And if it were so
Let him say to them
I hold, that is my view

phrases.english: And if it were so,
phrases.notes: He means: if רבי עקיבא really held like רבי שמעון everywhere.

phrases.english: let him say to them:
I, in the entire Torah,
hold like Rabbi Shimon!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the quote in step 11.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי עקיבא does not hold like רבי שמעון in general.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי עקיבא did not answer the רבנן by saying he follows רבי שמעון everywhere.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא was arguing on the Rabbis' own terms
steps.stepSummary: The proof from Step 12 is pushed off. Maybe רבי עקיבא does hold like רבי שמעון everywhere, but he answered the רבנן according to their own view.
steps.simpleTranslation: He was talking to the רבנן on their terms: 'For me, I hold like רבי שמעון in the whole תורה. But even for you, at least admit that since someone who clearly says it is liable, a plain oath is also liable!' And the רבנן said: No.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from Step 12. רבי עקיבא's silence does not show that he agrees with the רבנן in general.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא did not need to state his own general view, because the רבנן would not accept it anyway. So he argued from their own position: you agree that someone who clearly swears off 'any amount' is liable, so treat a plain oath the same way. The רבנן said no, so the argument stayed on that point.

keyTerms.meaning: According to their words, arguing from the other side's own position
For me / for you
At least admit to me
Clearly stated / plain, unspecified

steps.confusionAlert: The words 'I hold like רבי שמעון' are not something רבי עקיבא actually says in our משנה. The גמרא is suggesting what he could have meant, so that his silence proves nothing.

phrases.english: He was speaking to them according to the Rabbis' own words:
For me, in the entire Torah
I hold like Rabbi Shimon.
For you, at least admit to me
that since one who clearly specifies is liable,
one who swore plainly is also liable!
And the Rabbis said to him: No.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference drawn in Step 12
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof from רבי עקיבא's silence, not the question itself
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: His silence can be explained: he was arguing from the רבנן's own position, so it tells us nothing about his own general view.

steps.title: Proof from the נזיר who soaked bread in wine
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא says a נזיר is liable when bread and wine together add up to a כזית. If he held like רבי שמעון, why would he need them to add up?
steps.simpleTranslation: Come hear: רבי עקיבא says, a נזיר who soaked his bread in wine, and there is enough to add up to a כזית, is liable. If you think he holds like רבי שמעון in general, why does he need them to add up?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new proof that רבי עקיבא requires a כזית in general.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If any amount of wine made a נזיר liable, combining the bread with the wine to reach a כזית would not be needed. Since רבי עקיבא does talk about reaching a כזית, it seems he does require a כזית outside of oaths.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone who took a vow that forbids him wine
To combine, to add up together
And if it enters your mind (if you think that)

phrases.english: Come and hear: Rabbi Akiva says:
A nazir who soaked his bread in wine,

phrases.aramaic: וְיֵשׁ בָּהּ כְּדֵי לְצָרֵף כְּזַיִת – חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: and it has enough to combine into an olive-size, is liable.
phrases.notes: The wine alone is less than a כזית. It only reaches a כזית together with the bread.

phrases.english: And if you think
that in general he holds like Rabbi Shimon,
why do I need it to combine?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof was pushed off, a new proof is brought
steps.raayaObject: That רבי עקיבא requires a כזית in general, not like רבי שמעון
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי עקיבא's ruling about a נזיר who soaked bread in wine

steps.title: Another source: an oath not to eat, then eating forbidden foods
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה: someone swore not to eat, then ate non-kosher foods. The first opinion says he is liable; רבי שמעון exempts him.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we also learned: 'An oath that I will not eat,' and he ate נבלות, טרפות, שקצים and רמשים, he is liable. רבי שמעון exempts him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up another proof by quoting a משנה. The proof itself comes out of the discussion in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far this is only the base text. The גמרא will ask how the oath takes hold here, and one of the answers will involve רבי עקיבא's view.

keyTerms.meaning: And we also learned in a משנה
Animals that died without kosher slaughter, and fatally injured animals
Non-kosher creatures and creeping things
Exempts

phrases.english: And further, we learned:
"An oath that I will not eat,"
and he ate carcasses and fatally wounded animals,
repulsive creatures and creeping things, he is liable.
And Rabbi Shimon exempts him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a further source to support the same point
steps.raayaObject: That רבי עקיבא requires a כזית in general
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about an oath not to eat, followed by eating forbidden foods

steps.title: How can an oath take hold on food already forbidden?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why he is liable for the oath at all. He is already sworn from הר סיני not to eat these foods.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we discussed it: Why is he liable? He is already sworn from הר סיני!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a basic question on the משנה: an oath cannot add a prohibition to something the תורה already forbids.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Non-kosher food is already forbidden by the תורה, as if he were already under an oath. A new oath should not take hold on it, so how can he be liable for breaking his oath?

keyTerms.meaning: And we discussed it (raised a question on it)
Already sworn from Mount Sinai, already forbidden by the תורה

phrases.english: And we discussed it:
Why is he liable?
He is already sworn from Mount Sinai!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises a question on the משנה just quoted
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How an oath can take hold on foods already forbidden by the תורה
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that one who swore not to eat and then ate נבלות and טרפות is liable for the oath
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The food is already forbidden from הר סיני, and an oath cannot take hold on something already forbidden. So breaking this oath should bring no liability.

steps.title: Answer: he included permitted foods in the oath
steps.stepSummary: רב, שמואל and רבי יוחנן say the oath took hold because it included permitted foods together with the forbidden ones.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב, שמואל and רבי יוחנן all say: the case is where he included permitted things together with forbidden things.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the first answer to the question in Step 16.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the oath does take hold on the permitted foods, it takes hold on the forbidden ones along with them. This answer does not involve רבי עקיבא; it sets the stage for ריש לקיש's different answer.

keyTerms.meaning: Both of them (here meaning all of them together)
Includes, grouping several items into one oath
Permitted things / forbidden things

phrases.english: Rav and Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan
who all say:
phrases.notes: Literally 'both of them,' even though three names are listed. Here it just means they all agree.

phrases.english: It is where he includes permitted things
together with forbidden things.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן דְּאָמְרִי תַּרְוַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 16
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The oath includes permitted foods, so it takes hold on the forbidden foods along with them.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the oath also included permitted foods
steps.terutzMaskana: Because the oath takes hold on the permitted foods, it takes hold on the forbidden ones along with them.

steps.title: ריש לקיש's answer: a half-measure, using רבי עקיבא's view
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש says the oath takes hold only on less than a כזית: either he clearly swore off a half-measure (by the רבנן), or he swore plainly (by רבי עקיבא, who says a person forbids himself any amount).
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: You can only find it either when he clearly swore off a half-measure, according to the רבנן, or with a plain oath, according to רבי עקיבא, who says a person forbids himself any amount.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings ריש לקיש's different answer to the question in Step 16. It is the part that matters for our question about רבי עקיבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש's idea is that the oath takes hold on less than a כזית, because that small amount is not 'sworn from הר סיני.' For his second case to work, רבי עקיבא must hold that less than a כזית of forbidden food does not bring liability in the תורה. If it did, as רבי שמעון holds, the oath would have nothing to take hold on. This points to רבי עקיבא requiring a כזית in general.

keyTerms.meaning: You cannot find it except
A half-measure, less than the amount needed for liability (a כזית)
According to the view of
Forbids himself with even the smallest amount

steps.whatToRemember: ריש לקיש explains the plain oath by רבי עקיבא's view. That only works if, for רבי עקיבא, less than a כזית of forbidden food does not bring liability from the תורה. This is a strong hint that רבי עקיבא does not hold like רבי שמעון in general.
steps.whyThisMatters: ריש לקיש's answer ties straight back to the question from Step 8. It gives the גמרא another way to see what רבי עקיבא holds about forbidden foods in general.

phrases.english: And Reish Lakish said:
You cannot find it except
either where he clearly specifies a half-measure,
and according to the Rabbis,
or with a plain oath,
and according to Rabbi Akiva,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר: אָדָם אוֹסֵר עַצְמוֹ בְּכׇל שֶׁהוּא.
phrases.english: who says: a person forbids himself with any amount.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אָמַר: אִי אַתָּה מוֹצֵא אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, different answer to the question of Step 16
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The oath takes hold only on a half-measure: either clearly stated (by the רבנן) or plain (by רבי עקיבא).
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the oath takes hold only on a half-measure
steps.terutzMaskana: The oath takes hold on less than a כזית, which is not forbidden from הר סיני: either stated clearly (by the רבנן) or plain (by רבי עקיבא).

steps.title: If רבי עקיבא held like רבי שמעון, the oath could never take hold
steps.stepSummary: According to ריש לקיש, the oath takes hold on less than a כזית. If רבי עקיבא held like רבי שמעון that even a tiny amount is forbidden by the תורה, that tiny amount would already be sworn from הר סיני, and the oath could not take hold.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you think that in general he holds like רבי שמעון, then any amount is also already sworn from הר סיני!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is using ריש לקיש's answer from Step 18 to show that רבי עקיבא cannot hold like רבי שמעון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש said the oath only takes hold on less than a כזית, because that amount is not forbidden by the תורה. But רבי שמעון holds that any amount of forbidden food is forbidden. If רבי עקיבא agreed with him, there would be no amount left that is free from the תורה's prohibition, so the oath would have nothing to take hold on.

keyTerms.meaning: It enters your mind; you might think
In general; in other places
Any amount at all, even a tiny bit
Already under oath from הר סיני; already forbidden by the תורה, so a new oath cannot take hold

phrases.english: And if it enters your mind
that in general he holds like רבי שמעון,
then any amount, too,
is already sworn from Mount Sinai!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ בְּעָלְמָא כְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן סְבִירָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies ריש לקיש's explanation (Step 18) to prove the claim begun in Step 14.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי עקיבא does not hold like רבי שמעון in general.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ריש לקיש's statement that the oath takes hold only on less than a כזית.

steps.title: Conclusion: רבי עקיבא generally holds like the רבנן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that in general רבי עקיבא holds like the רבנן, that a כזית is needed for forbidden foods.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, must we not learn from this that in general he holds like the רבנן? Yes, learn from this.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the proof and accepts it: רבי עקיבא holds like the רבנן in general.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the רבי שמעון option fails, the only choice left is the רבנן's view: less than a כזית is not forbidden by the תורה. That is exactly the gap the oath can take hold on. רבי עקיבא's 'any amount' ruling is only about oaths, not about forbidden foods in general.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, is it not so that...? (leads to the only remaining option)
Learn from this; the proof is accepted
The Sages, the majority opinion

steps.whatToRemember: רבי עקיבא agrees with the רבנן that forbidden foods need a כזית. His 'any amount' rule is only about how people word oaths.

phrases.english: Rather, must we not learn from this:
that in general he holds like the Rabbis?
Learn from this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the proof in Step 19.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי עקיבא holds like the רבנן in general; his liability for any amount applies only to oaths.

steps.title: Quoting the רבנן's question to רבי עקיבא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: the רבנן asked רבי עקיבא where we ever find that eating any amount makes a person liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to רבי עקיבא: Where do we find, etc.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by quoting the רבנן's question from the משנה. This sets up the next move, where the גמרא tests that question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן argued that nowhere in the תורה is a person liable for eating a tiny amount, so he should not be liable here either. The גמרא is about to check whether that is really true.

keyTerms.meaning: Where do we find? (asking for a case like this elsewhere)
Etc.; the rest of the quote is assumed

phrases.english: They said to Rabbi Akiva:
phrases.notes: 'They' are the רבנן, in our משנה.

phrases.english: Where do we find, etc.
phrases.notes: The full line: where do we find that someone who eats any amount is liable, that this one should be liable?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ לְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא: הֵיכָן מָצִינוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the proof about רבי עקיבא's general view to the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The רבנן claim there is no case anywhere of liability for eating any amount.

steps.title: But someone who eats a whole ant is liable
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the רבנן's question: a person who eats an ant is liable, even though an ant is much smaller than a כזית.
steps.simpleTranslation: And do we not find it? But there is an ant!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the רבנן: there is a case of liability for less than a כזית, eating an ant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן said there is no such case anywhere. An ant is tiny, yet eating one is punishable. So it seems we do find liability for a tiny amount.

keyTerms.meaning: But there is...! (brings a counter-example)
An ant

phrases.english: And do we not?!
But there is an ant!
phrases.notes: Someone who eats a whole ant is liable, even though it is smaller than a כזית.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the claim quoted in Step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The רבנן's claim that no case of liability for a tiny amount exists.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An ant is less than a כזית, yet eating it brings liability.

steps.title: A whole creature is different
steps.stepSummary: Answer: an ant is a complete creature (בריה), which is important in itself, so it is not a case of plain 'any amount'.
steps.simpleTranslation: A whole creature is different.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ant case does not count, because a whole creature has its own importance.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Liability for the ant does not come from its size. It comes from the fact that it is a complete creature. A random tiny piece of food has no such importance, so the רבנן's question still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: A whole, complete creature, which counts as important no matter its size
Is different

phrases.english: A whole creature is different.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the ant challenge of Step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: the counter-example has a special feature.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ant shows liability for any tiny amount.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ant brings liability because it is a complete creature, not because tiny amounts count.

steps.title: But someone who eats הקדש is liable for less than a כזית
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges again: someone who eats הקדש (consecrated food) can be liable even for less than a כזית.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there is הקדש!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second example of liability for less than a כזית: eating הקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With הקדש, a person can be liable for eating less than a כזית. That looks like another case where a small amount brings liability.

keyTerms.meaning: Consecrated property belonging to the בית המקדש

phrases.english: But there is consecrated property!
phrases.notes: Someone who eats הקדש can be liable even for less than a כזית.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge to the רבנן's claim, after the ant was answered.
steps.kashyaTarget: The רבנן's claim that no case of liability for a tiny amount exists.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Eating הקדש brings liability even for less than a כזית.

steps.title: הקדש still needs a פרוטה's worth
steps.stepSummary: Answer: הקדש is not 'any amount'. It has its own minimum, the value of a פרוטה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we require a פרוטה's worth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that הקדש also has a minimum amount. It is measured by value instead of size.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Liability for הקדש needs food worth at least a פרוטה, even if that is smaller than a כזית. Since there is still a set minimum, it is not a case of 'any amount at all'.

keyTerms.meaning: We require
Worth a פרוטה, the smallest coin; the minimum for הקדש

phrases.english: But we require a peruta's worth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the הקדש challenge of Step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: the counter-example still has a set minimum.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: הקדש shows liability for any small amount.
steps.terutzMaskana: הקדש has a minimum of a פרוטה's worth, so it is not 'any amount'.

steps.title: But someone who clearly swore off any amount is liable
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges a third time: if someone clearly says in his oath that he will not eat even the smallest amount, he is liable for any amount.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there is one who specifies!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third example: a person who clearly swore not to eat even a tiny bit is liable for a tiny bit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees that if a person spells out 'not even a tiny amount', eating a tiny amount makes him liable. So it seems there is a case of liability for any amount.

keyTerms.meaning: One who spells out clearly (here, that even any amount is included in his oath)

phrases.english: But there is one who specifies!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third challenge, after the ant and הקדש were answered.
steps.kashyaTarget: The רבנן's claim that no case of liability for a tiny amount exists.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One who clearly swore off any amount is liable for any amount.

steps.title: Spelling it out makes it like a whole creature
steps.stepSummary: Answer: when a person clearly includes any amount in his oath, he gives that tiny amount importance, just like a whole creature.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who specifies is also like a whole creature.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that clearly swearing off any amount is like the ant case. The person himself made the tiny amount important.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בריה matters because it is complete. Here, the person's own clear words give the tiny amount importance. This is different from a plain oath, where nothing makes a tiny amount stand out, so the רבנן's question stays in place.

keyTerms.meaning: Is like; is comparable to

steps.whatToRemember: All three cases were turned away: the ant is a whole creature, הקדש has a פרוטה minimum, and clearly swearing off any amount is like a whole creature. The רבנן's question 'where do we find it?' still stands.

phrases.english: One who specifies, too,
is like a whole creature.
phrases.notes: By spelling it out, he made the tiny amount important, just as a whole creature is important.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 26 by comparing it to the answer of Step 23.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Clearly swearing off any amount shows that tiny amounts bring liability.
steps.terutzMaskana: The person's clear words give the tiny amount importance, like a בריה, so it is not a plain 'any amount' case.

steps.title: A fourth challenge from the case of dirt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges its approach again with the case of someone who swore not to eat and then ate dirt.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what about dirt?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a fourth case, dirt (עפר), to challenge the approach it has been defending.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each earlier challenge got its own answer: an ant is a whole creature (בריה), הקדש has its own minimum of a פרוטה, and a clear oath gives a tiny amount importance. Dirt does not seem to fit any of these answers, so the approach is in trouble again.

keyTerms.meaning: But look at / but what about (opens a challenge from a known case)
Dirt, earth

steps.confusionAlert: This line is very short. The whole challenge is just the word 'dirt'. The learner has to supply the logic: dirt is a case that none of the earlier answers covers.

phrases.english: But what about dirt?!
phrases.notes: The case of someone who swore not to eat and then ate dirt. It is not a whole creature, not הקדש, and nobody said 'any amount'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the third counter-example was answered in step 27, the גמרא raises a fourth counter-example to the רבנן's claim, one that the earlier answers do not cover.
steps.kashyaTarget: The רבנן's claim in the משנה (step 21) that we never find liability for eating any amount
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Dirt has no special importance. It is not a whole creature, has no value-based minimum, and was not singled out in the oath. So none of the earlier answers explains it.

steps.title: The גמרא begins to restate the רבנן's question
steps.stepSummary: With the word 'אלא' the גמרא signals that it is giving up its current line and is about to offer a different explanation.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather...
steps.whatsHappening: This step is a setup. The גמרא says 'rather', which tells us it is setting up a new explanation that will continue in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dirt case cannot be explained away like the ant, הקדש or a clearly stated oath. So with 'אלא' the גמרא starts rewording what the רבנן's question 'היכן מצינו' really meant. The new wording continues on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (drops what was said before and opens a new approach)

steps.whatToRemember: When the גמרא says 'אלא' right after a challenge, it usually means: 'that approach didn't work, so let's try a different one.'

phrases.english: Rather,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the dirt challenge by abandoning the earlier line of answers.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Retraction and restart: the earlier approach is dropped in favor of a new one, still to come.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The רבנן's question means there is no case anywhere of liability for any amount, and each counter-example can be explained away one at a time.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because dirt cannot be explained away that way, the רבנן's question has to be worded differently. The new wording continues on the next amud.
